title: How a song-recognition app works

segments.text: How does an app recognise a song in seconds?
It throws away almost all of the music.
Step one: it turns the sound into a spectrogram, a picture of which pitches are loud at each moment.
Step two: it keeps only the loudest peaks. What's left looks like a map of stars.
Step three: it joins pairs of stars into fingerprints: two pitches, and the time between them.
Then it looks them up in a huge library of songs.
The match is the song where your fingerprints line up at the same spacing. Even if only one or two percent survive the noise, it can still find it.
So it isn't listening to the tune. It's matching stars.
Send this to a music lover.

sources: Avery Li-Chun Wang (Shazam Entertainment), 'An Industrial-Strength Audio Search Algorithm', ISMIR 2003, https://www.ee.columbia.edu/~dpwe/papers/Wang03-shazam.pdf: spectrogram peaks chosen by amplitude reduce 'a complicated spectrogram' to 'a sparse set of coordinates' called 'constellation maps' because they 'often resemble a star field' (2.1)

Same paper 2.2: 'pairs of time-frequency points are combinatorially associated. Anchor points are chosen, each anchor point having a target zone'; each hash is built from the two frequencies and the time difference between the points

Same paper 2.3: hashes are searched in the database; for the matching song, matching features 'occur at similar relative offsets' and form 'a diagonal line within the scatterplot'; the score is the number of matching, time-aligned hashes
Same paper 3.1: 'from a heavily corrupted 15 second sample, a statistically significant match can be determined with only about 1-2% of the generated hash tokens actually surviving'
Same paper 1 and 3.1: users sample up to 15 seconds; tests used 15, 10 and 5 second excerpts (basis for 'in seconds')
